concepts.title: Sensing and Responding to the Environment
concepts.definition: Organisms constantly take in signals from their surroundings through senses and receptors and respond to them - plants bend toward light, animals flee danger - and such stimulus-response pairs keep living beings tuned to a changing world.
concepts.key_idea: Detect the signal, answer it: sensitivity to stimuli is a signature of life.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu112.txt lines 61-150 (how do we experience and interpret the environment)
question_patterns: how do organisms respond to changes in their surroundings
give two examples of plants responding to light or touch
what is a stimulus - define with an example
how do animals use their senses to survive
why is responding to the environment important for life
compare how humans and plants react to stimuli

solution_steps.explain: Senses or receptors pick up light, sound, touch, chemicals or temperature.
The body interprets the signal and prepares a reaction.
Movement, growth or behaviour changes complete the response.

concepts.title: Living Together: Populations and Communities
concepts.definition: Nature is organised into shared neighbourhoods: all members of one species in an area form a population, and populations of plants, animals and microbes living together in that area make a community, each member finding food and shelter there.
concepts.key_idea: One species together is a population; many species together is a community.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu112.txt lines 150-215 (who all live together in nature)
question_patterns: define population and community with examples from a pond
who all live together in a forest community
how is a population different from a community
name the members of a garden community
why do different organisms share the same habitat
arrange individual, population and community in order of size

solution_steps.explain: All individuals of one kind in an area form its population.
Populations of all species sharing the habitat build the community.
Together with soil, water and air, the community lives in an ecosystem.

concepts.title: Interactions Among Organisms
concepts.definition: Organisms interact in many ways: some cooperate in mutualism where both gain, some compete for the same food or light, while others live as parasites or predators and prey - each interaction shapes who thrives in a community.
concepts.key_idea: Win-win, win-lose or rivalry - interactions steer the life of a community.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu112.txt lines 265-471 (types of interactions in a community)
question_patterns: name the different types of interactions between organisms
what is mutualism - give an example
how does competition arise in a community
distinguish a parasite from a predator
describe the relationship between a bee and a flower
how do interactions decide which organisms survive

solution_steps.explain: Decide whether both benefit, one suffers, or both are harmed.
Mutualism, competition, predation and parasitism label the common patterns.
Each interaction changes population sizes and community balance.

concepts.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
concepts.definition: Energy from the sun flows through a community along eating links: green plants trap sunlight as producers, herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat herbivores, and interconnected chains weave into a food web that shows who eats whom.
concepts.key_idea: Sun to plant to animal to hunter: every meal passes energy one link along.
question_patterns: what is a food chain - draw one from a grassland
who are producers in a food chain and why
distinguish herbivores, carnivores and omnivores
how does a food web differ from a food chain
what happens to a food chain if one member disappears
trace the energy flow from the sun to a lion

solution_steps.explain: Green plants capture solar energy and make food.
Herbivores feed on plants, carnivores on herbivores, forming a chain.
Overlapping chains of a community form its food web.

concepts.title: Decomposers and the Balance of Nature
concepts.definition: Nothing is wasted in nature: decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead bodies and droppings into soil nutrients that plants reuse, while feedback among populations keeps numbers in check - nature's recycling and harmony at work.
concepts.key_idea: Decomposers return matter to the soil, closing the loop that keeps ecosystems going.
concepts.textbook_ref: hecu112.txt lines 589-741 (waste in nature, change, balance)
question_patterns: what happens to dead plants and animals in a forest
who are decomposers - give two examples
how do nutrients return to the soil in nature
why is nature said to maintain a balance
what would happen if decomposers disappeared
explain the recycling of matter in an ecosystem

solution_steps.explain: Fungi and bacteria break dead matter into simple substances.
Plants absorb these nutrients, restarting the food chain.
Predation, competition and food supply hold populations in check.

concepts.title: Ecosystems and Their Benefits
concepts.definition: A community together with its non-living surroundings - soil, water, air, light - works as an ecosystem; forests, ponds and grasslands supply food, water purification, climate control and countless other services on which human life depends.
concepts.key_idea: Living community plus physical surroundings equals ecosystem - nature's service provider.
question_patterns: what is an ecosystem - name its living and non-living parts
give two examples of ecosystems
list the benefits that a forest ecosystem gives us
how does a pond work as an ecosystem
why should ecosystems be protected
which non-living factors shape an ecosystem

solution_steps.action: add the surroundings to the community
solution_steps.explain: Living organisms plus air, water, soil and light form the ecosystem.
Food, clean water, fertile soil and moderated climate flow from ecosystems.
Damaging one part weakens the services, so conservation protects human welfare too.
